catalog_quote: Pa (also known as Pare) is spoken by about 1,500 people living between the Elevala River and Lake Murray, west of the Strickland River. ... In a preliminary analysis of the sound system the following phonemes have been tentatively identified: p, t, k, b [b, β], d [ⁿd, d], g [g, ɣ], (f [pᶲ, ɸ]), s [ᵗs, s], h, m, n, (ŋ), r [ř], w, y; i [i, ɩ], e [e, ě], ɛ [ɛ, æ], a [a, ɑ], ɔ [ɒ, ɔ], o [o, ɤ], u [u, ɯ], (ə). Five of the eight vowels also occur nasalized, but the phonemic status of the nasalized vowels is still uncertain. There is some evidence that the language has contrastive pitch, possibly a high and a low tone.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (116 pp., chapter runs 345-460) and rendered p. 46 = printed p. 390; the text (txt l. 2215-2231) and the page scan both carry sec. 2.6.2.2.6.4.2 'Pa'. The load-bearing sentence is on the page exactly as quoted: 'There is some evidence that the language has contrastive pitch, possibly a high and a low tone.' The opening sentence ('Pa (also known as Pare) is spoken by about 1,500 people living between the Elevala River and Lake Murray, west of the Strickland River.') and the nasalized-vowel sentence are also verbatim. Minor differences are confined to the compiler de-spaced phoneme list: the page reads d [ⁿd, d], s [ᵗs, s], (f [pᶲ, ɸ]), r [ř], e [e, ě] where the report has d [d, nd], s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given anywhere in print. Voorhoeve's preliminary analysis reports possible contrastive pitch (a high and a low tone) and says nothing about stress; Suter & Usher 2017 repeat this (tonal, tone untranscribed) and confirm that no grammatical or phonological description of Pa exists in print.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the tone claim itself is hedged ('some evidence', 'possibly'). Usher (New Guinea World) paraphrases it as 'suggested but not affirmed'.
new_statements.domain_note: Preliminary survey-chapter sketch based on Voorhoeve's own 1966-1974 fieldwork on the easternmost (Ba) dialect (Voorhoeve 1968: 6); elicited wordlist forms, no phrase-level discussion. The saved scanned text is letter-spaced; the quote above is the de-spaced reading of the text layerIPA symbols restored from the page scan where the scanned garbled them (β, ɸ, ɣ, ɺ, ŋ, ə).
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes 'Pa (also known as Pare)' = pare1271 [ppt]; Voorhoeve's own data come from the easternmost 'Ba' dialect (Voorhoeve 1968: 6). Do not confuse with (a) the Aekyom dialect 'Aekyom-Pare' / 'Akium-Pare' (Southeastern Aekyom, under aeky1238), 'Pare' being the Aekyom exonym for the Pa people (Depew 1986: 330 via Suter & Usher 2017: 107), or (b) Pare/Asu of Tanzania (Bantu). The Kamula stress statements held in (Routamaa & Routamaa 1995: penultimate) concern kamu1260, a different language of the same family.

sources.citation: Suter, Edgar & Timothy Usher. 2017. The Kamula-Elevala language family. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia 35: 106-131.
sources.note: p. 108: Pa is 'the least well described' KE language, 'only lexical data is available but no description of the grammar'; the Rule grammar and phonology papers for Pa were never published and could not be located. p. 109: 'The languages are tonal, but the lexical data we have for them does not include a transcription of tone.' p. 110: 'Voorhoeve (1975: 390) mentions that Pa has contrastive pitch, but tones are not represented in Waldeck's orthography.' p. 116: 'The role stress played in the history of the Kamula-Elevala languages is not well understood'; p. 120: stress cannot be reconstructed…
